Patient: Baby Boy Ellison        MRN: 00-DEMO-4471        Sex: Male
DOB: 2026-03-02 (DOL 0)      Location: NICU, Bed 12
Attending: A. Okafor, MD         Author: R. Patel, MD (Neonatology)
Note type: NICU Admission Note (History & Physical)               Date/Time: 2026-03-02 03:40
------------------------------------------------------------------------

CHIEF COMPLAINT
Respiratory distress and inability to pass a nasogastric catheter shortly
after birth.

HISTORY OF PRESENT ILLNESS
Baby Boy Ellison is a 37+2 week male infant delivered by spontaneous vaginal
delivery to a 31-year-old G2P1 mother whose pregnancy was complicated by
polyhydramnios. Apgars were 6 and 8. In the delivery room the infant became
dusky with quiet handling and pinked up promptly with vigorous crying; the
team was unable to pass a suction catheter through either naris, raising
concern for bilateral choanal atresia. A grade III/VI systolic murmur was
appreciated at the left sternal border, and a congenital heart defect was
suspected pending echocardiography. The infant did not pass the newborn
hearing screen in either ear. On penlight examination the bedside team noted
a possible coloboma of the right iris; ophthalmology was consulted for formal
evaluation.

PHYSICAL EXAMINATION
General: alert, mildly dysmorphic term-appearing male.
HEENT: cup-shaped, low-set external ears bilaterally. There was no cleft lip
  or palate on direct visualization and palpation. An oral airway was placed
  to relieve obstruction during quiet periods.
Cardiac: regular rhythm with the murmur described above.
Genitourinary: both testes were undescended in the inguinal canals.
Neuro: the infant was diffusely hypotonic with reduced spontaneous movement.

ASSESSMENT & PLAN
Late-preterm male with multiple congenital anomalies concerning for an
underlying genetic syndrome. Genetics and Cardiology consulted. NG tube placed
for feeds. Continue cardiorespiratory monitoring.

Note type: Progress Note (SOAP)               Date/Time: 2026-03-06 07:15
------------------------------------------------------------------------

SUBJECTIVE
DOL 4. Infant tolerating continuous NG feeds with intermittent oxygen
desaturations during handling. Nursing reports intermittent nystagmus noted at
the bedside overnight.

OBJECTIVE
Exam notable for persistent central hypotonia with head lag on pull-to-sit.
Attempts at oral feeding were poorly coordinated and the infant demonstrated
dysphagia with pooling of secretions, so he remains NG-dependent. A head
ultrasound obtained yesterday showed no evidence of intraventricular
hemorrhage. Morning labs revealed an ionized calcium of 0.92 mmol/L,
consistent with hypocalcemia, and calcium supplementation was started.

ASSESSMENT & PLAN
Ongoing multisystem workup as below. Continue NG feeds and monitor closely for
aspiration during any oral feeding trials. Repeat calcium this evening.
Awaiting genetics and cardiology recommendations.

*** SYNTHETIC DEMONSTRATION RECORD - NOT A REAL PATIENT ***
Patient: Baby Boy Ellison        MRN: 00-DEMO-4471        Sex: Male
DOB: 2026-03-02 (DOL 5)      Location: NICU, Bed 12
Attending: A. Okafor, MD         Author: S. Ibarra, MD (Medical Genetics)
Note type: Genetics Consult Note               Date/Time: 2026-03-07 14:20
------------------------------------------------------------------------

REASON FOR CONSULT
Multiple congenital anomalies, evaluate for a unifying genetic diagnosis.

FINDINGS
We examined the infant and reviewed imaging and subspecialty input.
Nasal endoscopy by ENT confirmed bilateral choanal atresia. Ophthalmology's
dilated exam demonstrated bilateral chorioretinal coloboma. There was a
left-sided facial weakness producing an asymmetric crying facies, consistent
with a cranial nerve VII palsy. The external ears were cup-shaped with
deficient earlobes, and an auditory brainstem response study was consistent
with bilateral sensorineural hearing loss. CT of the temporal bones showed
hypoplasia of both semicircular canals. Both testes remained undescended,
confirming bilateral cryptorchidism.

FAMILY HISTORY
There is one older sibling who underwent repair of a cleft lip in infancy. The
mother has hypothyroidism managed with levothyroxine. No family history of
sudden death or consanguinity.

IMPRESSION
The constellation of coloboma, choanal atresia, cranial nerve dysfunction,
characteristic external ears with sensorineural hearing loss, semicircular
canal hypoplasia, and genital hypoplasia meets clinical criteria for CHARGE
syndrome. CHD7 sequencing has been sent.

DOB: 2026-03-02 (DOL 5)      Location: NICU, Bed 12
Attending: A. Okafor, MD         Author: D. Cho, MD (Pediatric Cardiology)
Note type: Cardiology Consult Note               Date/Time: 2026-03-07 16:45
------------------------------------------------------------------------

REASON FOR CONSULT
Systolic murmur and suspected structural heart disease.

ECHOCARDIOGRAM
The transthoracic echocardiogram demonstrated a large malaligned
ventricular septal defect with an overriding aorta, right ventricular
outflow tract obstruction, and right ventricular hypertrophy - findings
diagnostic of tetralogy of Fallot. A small patent ductus arteriosus was
also present with left-to-right flow. Biventricular systolic function was
preserved.

ASSESSMENT & PLAN
Tetralogy of Fallot with currently balanced physiology and adequate
saturations off prostaglandin. No immediate intervention required. We will
follow serially for progression of outflow obstruction and coordinate
surgical timing with the multidisciplinary team given the broader syndromic
picture.

Attending: A. Okafor, MD         Author: R. Patel, MD (Neonatology)
Note type: Discharge Summary               Date/Time: 2026-03-28 11:00
------------------------------------------------------------------------

HOSPITAL COURSE
Baby Boy Ellison was admitted at birth with respiratory obstruction and
multiple congenital anomalies. Bilateral choanal atresia was confirmed and
stented by ENT. CHD7 sequencing returned a pathogenic variant, confirming a
molecular diagnosis of CHARGE syndrome. His cardiac lesion was characterized
as tetralogy of Fallot, which remained stable off prostaglandin throughout
admission. Feeding was limited by ongoing dysphagia; after a failed oral
feeding trial a gastrostomy tube was placed, and caregivers were trained on
tube feeds with continued precautions for aspiration. Audiology reconfirmed
bilateral sensorineural hearing loss and arranged early-intervention
follow-up. Bilateral cryptorchidism will be followed by urology as an
outpatient.

DISCHARGE DIAGNOSES
1. CHARGE syndrome (pathogenic CHD7 variant)
2. Tetralogy of Fallot
3. Bilateral chorioretinal coloboma
4. Bilateral choanal atresia, stented
5. Bilateral sensorineural hearing loss
6. Dysphagia, G-tube dependent
7. Bilateral cryptorchidism

DISCHARGE PLAN
Home on G-tube feeds with cardiology, genetics, ENT, audiology, ophthalmology,
and urology follow-up.

test.title: Test Note One - Joe Smith MD
test.html:
Overview of Rare Syndromes and Associated Anomalies

This document provides an overview of complex syndromes, including detailed descriptions of symptoms, associated conditions, and key characteristics for better understanding.

Megalencephaly-Polymicrogyria-Polydactyly-Hydrocephalus (MPPH) Syndrome

MPPH syndrome is a complex condition involving various congenital anomalies and developmental issues. Key characteristics include:

  • Bilateral polymicrogyria and cortical dysplasia
  • Post-axial polysyndactyly of hands and feet
  • Macrosomia affecting both head size and overall length
  • Hypotonia and global developmental delays
  • Hydrocephalus contributing to increased head size

Multiple Congenital Anomalies

This term refers to the presence of multiple birth defects involving different organ systems. Commonly associated conditions include:

  • Tetralogy of Fallot, a complex congenital heart defect
  • Brain anomalies, including polymicrogyria and hydrocephalus
  • Post-axial polydactyly and syndactyly
  • Macrocephaly and disproportionate growth patterns

Management often requires a multidisciplinary approach involving cardiology, neurology, orthopedics, and genetic counseling.

Detailed Case Study: Tetralogy of Fallot

Tetralogy of Fallot is characterized by four distinct cardiac anomalies:

  1. Ventricular septal defect (VSD)
  2. Pulmonary stenosis
  3. Overriding aorta
  4. Right ventricular hypertrophy

Early surgical intervention is critical for survival and improving long-term outcomes.

Associated Brain Anomalies

In MPPH syndrome, brain anomalies are a hallmark feature, including:

  • Polymicrogyria: An abnormal organization of the brain's cortical layers
  • Hydrocephalus: Excess cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) within the brain's ventricles
  • Cortical dysplasia: Disruption of normal brain structure and function

These anomalies contribute to cognitive and developmental delays, as well as seizures in some cases.

Macrosomia and Growth Patterns

Macrosomia in MPPH syndrome is defined by:

  • Significant enlargement of the head circumference (macrocephaly)
  • Increased body length relative to age-matched peers
  • Disproportionate growth patterns affecting overall symmetry

Monitoring growth is critical for early intervention and management of associated complications.

Developmental Delays and Hypotonia

Children with MPPH syndrome often exhibit:

  • Global developmental delays impacting motor and cognitive milestones
  • Hypotonia, resulting in reduced muscle strength and tone
  • Speech and language delays requiring therapy

Intervention programs, including physical and occupational therapy, are vital to support development.

test.text: A 44-year- old super-morbidly- obese man body mass index (BMI 63) underwent sleeve gastrectomy for weight loss and was found to have multiple adenomatous fundic gland polyps on final pathology. Subsequent workup included esophagogastroduodenoscopy which revealed innumerable polyps of the remaining gastric fundus and body consistent with fundic gland polyps, normal duodenum without polyps, and Barrett’s oesophagus. Colonoscopy was significant for innumerable polyps of varying sizes up to 1.5 cm throughout the colon, with relative rectal sparing. Biopsies were consistent with tubular adenoma and hyperplastic polyps. Thyroid ultrasound was within normal limits and abdominal CT was significant for left-sided 3.4 cm mesenteric mass representing scarring versus possible desmoid. Family history was significant for colon cancer diagnosed in his maternal grandfather at age 72, paternal grandmother who died of metastatic cancer at age 50 with unknown primary and mother diagnosed with thyroid cancer at age 40. Physical examination was notable for morbid obesity (BMI 45), cardiopulmonary examination within normal limits and abdomen with well-healing surgical scars from prior sleeve gastrectomy.

test.text:
Progress Note — Pediatric Genetics / Multisystem Evaluation

HPI: Patient is a young child referred for multisystem concerns. On exam the patient has low muscle tone and an unusually small head. Parents report he has difficulty swallowing and the baby has trouble feeding and often spits up. He experiences frequent headaches per mom, and has poor coordination noted both at home and in clinic.

Growth & Development: The patient is short for his age. He stopped meeting milestones and lost skills he had. His speech is hard to understand even for family, and he can't keep up with other kids on the playground.

Cardiopulmonary: He gets winded climbing a single flight of stairs. There have been repeated chest infections since birth.

HEENT / Sensory: Her hearing has gotten noticeably worse over the past year. Her vision is blurry and getting worse.

Musculoskeletal / Skin: There is curvature of the spine. The patient's muscles have been wasting away. Skin is very stretchy and joints bend too far.

Abdominal: The child has an enlarged liver.

Heme: He bruises very easily.

Pertinent negatives: The patient does not have seizures. There is no evidence of hearing loss on formal screening today. We initially suspected ataxia, but this was not confirmed.

Family history: His brother has cystic fibrosis, but the patient is unaffected.

test.text: The first case was the second child of healthy non-consanguineous parents of Palestinian origin. She was born at 32 weeks gestation, weighing 1.800 kg via normal vaginal delivery, and required admission to the Neonatal unit for prematurity and respiratory distress. At 5 months of age, she was admitted to the pediatric ward due to recurrent vomiting, poor weight gain, and chronic constipation of 2 months duration. Physical examination showed a dehydrated, pale, cachectic infant, with poor eye contact but normal power and tone. Laboratory tests showed leukopenia, anemia, salt wasting, renal failure with elevated blood lactate, marked hyperuricemia, hypercholesterolemia, and hypertriglyceridemia. Abdominal ultrasound showed normal kidneys, heart echocardiography revealed no pulmonary hypertension. Moreover, Her clinical condition gradually deteriorated and within a few weeks of admission, she was in multiorgan failure, reached end-stage renal failure and regular peritoneal dialysis was initiated. At 12 months of age, the patient died after developing respiratory failure. Whole exome sequencing showed a homozygous variant in the SARS2 gene (c.1175A>G (p. Asp392Gly)), defined as a pathogenic variant according to the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG) classification
